text: Everything you've touched so far in this course lives as a row in a table, built on ServiceNow's underlying Glide data model. That part sounds like any ordinary relational database. But here's what's genuinely different: in ServiceNow, a table isn't just a structure the database engine knows about. A table is itself represented by an actual record, sitting in another table, that you can open, read, and edit through the ordinary user interface, no SQL required.

Every table in the entire instance, including the one that stores this very fact, has exactly one row in a table called sys_db_object. That row carries the table's real database name, like incident, its human-readable label, and which table it extends. When you navigate to System Definition, then Tables, you're looking at a list view built directly on sys_db_object — one row per table across the whole platform, from core admin tables down to anything custom you build yourself.

A table's columns aren't baked into a fixed schema file either. Each column, which ServiceNow calls a field, is its own record in a table called sys_dictionary, pointing back at the table it belongs to, and carrying that field's name, label, data type, length, and default value. Opening a table's Columns related list is really just querying sys_dictionary for every entry whose table reference matches. Chapter 4 goes much deeper on the dictionary.

When any table is created, ServiceNow automatically adds a set of standard fields no admin ever has to define by hand. sys_id is a 32-character GUID that becomes that record's permanent, unique primary key. sys_created_on and sys_created_by get stamped once, at creation. sys_updated_on and sys_updated_by refresh on every single save, and sys_mod_count keeps a running tally of how many times the record has changed.

Because structure itself is metadata, not a fixed schema file, you can add a brand-new field to any table through the UI — no DDL, no migration script, no server restart required. ServiceNow simply reads sys_dictionary live, and that new field is immediately available everywhere the table is used. That one capability is the foundation this entire chapter, and most of platform administration, builds on. Next up: how one table extends another.
